newsitem.title: UK: British press derides view of Queen as "lefty".
newsitem.headline: British press derides view of Queen as "lefty".

text.p: A new biography of Queen Elizabeth that claims she has used her influence to push government policy to the left was derided as fantasy on Friday by Britain's right-wing press.

Ben Pimlott's "The Queen: A Biography of Elizabeth II" is based on interviews with royal family members and courtiers, plus "unprecedented access to the royal archives", according to the Independent newspaper, which began serialisation this week.
Pimlott told the Independent that the Queen was "in her own way a bit of a lefty", but rival biographer Sarah Bradford dismissed that as ludicrous in the right-wing Daily Express.
"She is officially and constitutionally apolitical, but all the evidence goes to show that she is conservative with a small "c'," Bradford said.
Buckingham Palace refused to comment on the book.
Pimlott says her left-leaning views were clear, if subtle, and were, as the Independent put it, "not confined to attempts to temper the excesses of the later years of Thatcherism".

She was angry at former premier Margaret Thatcher's support for the U.S. invasion of Grenada in 1983 and doubted the wisdom of allowing Washington to use British airbases for a raid on Libya in 1986, he claims.

She did not agree with Thatcher's opposition to sanctions against the apartheid regime in South Africa, and was worried about the social effects of government policy, in particular its handling of the year-long miners' strike in 1984-85.

Many commentators before have spoken of the frosty relationship between Thatcher and the queen, although Simon Heffer, writing in the right-wing Daily Mail, said the queen's "supposed antipathy" to Thatcher had been repeatedly denied.
But Heffer notes the queen was uncomfortable with Thatcher's policies and more at home with the paternalism of her more aristocratic predecessors, like Harold Macmillan.
"If the queen is to be categorised politically, she is much more a Tory of the old, pre-Thatcher school," he said.
Royal biographer Bradford agreed, describing the queen as a "Tory wet" -- Thatcher's dismissive term for Conservatives opposed to her crusade against public spending and trade unions.
The Daily Telegraph said she was "neither Left nor Right of centre but, in the broadest possible sense, the centre itself".
Christopher Hudson in the London Evening Standard said the examples of regal interference listed by Pimlott might better be seen as simple common sense.
"Economic sanctions against South Africa, as we all now know, in the end had the desired effect," Hudson said, somewhat at variance with the Standard line at the time.
All the same, he called the notion of the queen being left-wing "delightfully fantastical".
"The queen comes from one of the most instinctively Conservative families in Britain," he added, dismissing the "closet lefty" thesis as nothing more than a marketing ploy.
